title: A Conversation That Leads Somewhere
summary: Explore listening, feedback, disagreement, and repair through a difficult conversation with a partner.
learningObjective: Explore listening, feedback, disagreement, and repair through a difficult conversation with a partner.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Let's start with a conversation many teams recognize. A partner says, we keep giving you feedback, but nothing happens. You're the supervisor receiving that message. Where do you begin?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd be tempted to list all the meetings we've held. But that wouldn't answer what happened to their feedback. I'd ask which concern they want us to follow up on.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Right. Inviting people to a meeting and responding to their input are different things. Before we talk, I'd check the comments, the decision, and what can still change.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: And who can change it. I don't want to offer something beyond my authority just to make the conversation easier.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: The partner explains that they asked for a clearer contact route in a service guide. The final guide still has the old wording, and they never heard why. How could you check your understanding?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd say, you want to know how that comment was considered, and you haven't received an explanation. Have I got that right? Then I'd give them room to correct me.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: That last part is important. A summary is an invitation to clarify. If they correct it, we need to use the correction, rather than return to the defense we'd already prepared.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: What about speaking with the colleague who handled the comments? We still need to discuss responsibility.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: We do. Start with what you can establish. The reviewer saw the comments after approval. Ask what happened between receipt and forwarding. Was the expected handoff clear? Then discuss the action and its effect.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: That gives the colleague a chance to explain without turning the conversation into a judgment about their character. If the expectation was clear and it wasn't met, we can address that directly too.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Now the team disagrees. One person wants to hold the whole guide. Another says we must release it today. How do you keep the conversation useful?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd bring it back to the particular instruction. What could happen if it stays unclear? Can the responsible team confirm the correction today? What needs an approval decision? That gives us something more useful than arguing about who cares most.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: And we can acknowledge the pressure. People may have worked hard against a deadline. That effort matters, and so does the person trying to use the guide.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Suppose we did miss the comment. I'd want to say that plainly: we missed your concern, and you should have received an answer. Here's what we're doing now.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Yes. A direct acknowledgment doesn't need a long explanation of our good intentions. Follow it with a correction you can make, or the route for a decision. The partner doesn't have to reassure us before we help.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: They might still be disappointed. We can respect that and keep doing the work. We shouldn't ask for forgiveness as a condition of moving forward.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: What would you change before the next review?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd name who responds to comments and when, allow written input as well as discussion, and explain the final decision. A short follow-up can say what changed, what didn't, and why.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: For your own practice, choose one conversation coming up. Write an opening question that helps you understand the concern. Then name one commitment you can actually keep. You can pause and rehearse it in your own words.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: And after the conversation, ask yourself: can the other person tell what happened to their concern? That question can help staff and leaders turn a difficult exchange into useful guidance and dependable follow-through.
